opus-5.5.text:
Around 2019 and 2020, you could really feel something changing in the U.S. labs. During my PhD at Stanford I worked mostly on 3D vision: object pose estimation, category-level understanding, point clouds. A lot of us in that community started asking: we can perceive the 3D world better and better, but what is it *for*? The natural answer was interaction. A robot has to see an object, understand its geometry and parts, and then actually manipulate it.

So the center of gravity was moving from passive perception toward what people started calling embodied AI. Simulation environments for robot learning were appearing, interactive datasets were being built, and more vision people were attending robotics conferences and vice versa. It felt like the boundary between computer vision and robotics was dissolving.

When I was deciding to come back to China, that trend was a big part of my thinking. I felt this direction would be one of the most important of the next ten years. It was still early, the problems were wide open, and nobody had a dominant position yet. China also had something special: a very strong manufacturing base and hardware supply chain. Embodied AI is not purely an algorithm problem. Eventually you need real robots, real hands, real deployment, and doing that close to the supply chain is a huge advantage.

There was also a talent side. At that time, very few faculty in China were focused specifically on embodied AI. I thought if I went back to Peking University and built a lab around this direction early, I could train a group of students who would grow up with the field. Honestly, it was a bit of a bet. In 2020 many people still thought robotics was slow, hard, and not very "AI." But I believed the convergence of 3D vision, simulation, and learning would make general-purpose robots possible, and I wanted to be part of building it from the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response describes computer vision researchers moving toward embodied AI and mentions robotics, but it does not identify reinforcement learning researchers as part of the convergence or connect that convergence to taking faculty positions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at that time I don't think most people were using the phrase "embodied AI" yet, at least not the way we use it now. What I saw around 2019 and 2020, while I was finishing my PhD at Stanford and working with Leonidas Guibas, was more of a quiet convergence. The 3D vision community, the robotics community, and the deep learning community were starting to run into each other's problems.

In 3D vision, we had gotten pretty good at understanding static scenes, estimating pose, segmenting objects, reconstructing geometry. But a lot of us started asking: what is this understanding for? If a model can tell me the 6D pose of a mug, the natural next question is, can a robot pick it up? And once you ask that, you realize perception alone is not enough. You need to reason about affordances, about articulated parts, about how things move when you interact with them. That pulled vision people toward robotics.

At the same time, people coming from reinforcement learning were hitting a wall in simulation. Policies trained in toy environments did not transfer. They needed richer 3D assets, better physics, more realistic sensors. So they were pulled toward the graphics and 3D vision side. You saw this in the kind of work coming out of Stanford, Berkeley, MIT, and in projects like PartNet and SAPIEN that I was involved in. The datasets themselves were telling you where the field was going, because they were built around interaction rather than recognition.

So when I was deciding to come back to China, my read was that this wasn't a fashion. It was a structural shift. The low-hanging fruit in passive perception was mostly picked, and the next hard problems were about agents that act in the physical world. That is a long-horizon bet, and it requires a lot of infrastructure, hardware, simulation, and patient funding.

Returning to Peking University made sense to me for a few reasons. One, this direction needs scale, and China has a very strong manufacturing and robotics supply chain, so it is realistic to go from research to actual robots. Two, I felt the Chinese academic community in 3D vision and robotics was still relatively young, and there was room to help shape how the field grows here rather than only follow. And three, frankly, I thought the window was open. The people who positioned themselves early in this convergence would have an advantage that compounds over years.

Of course, in 2020 there was also uncertainty from the pandemic and from U.S.–China tensions, which made the decision feel more urgent. But I would say the primary driver was intellectual. I believed the center of gravity in AI was moving from understanding the world to acting in it, and I wanted to build a group around that from the ground up.

r001.rationale: The response describes a 2019–20 convergence between 3D vision, robotics, and reinforcement learning toward embodied AI. It does not connect that convergence to researchers pursuing the direction when taking faculty positions.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I’d describe it as a shift in the questions researchers were asking. It wasn’t just, “Can an AI recognize what’s in an image?” It was, “Can it understand enough about the world to act in it?” Once you ask that, perception becomes connected to movement, interaction, and the consequences of an action.

I wouldn’t say there was already a clear consensus in 2020. But that direction made embodied AI an exciting area to think about: intelligence that learns through interacting with the physical world. In the context of returning to China, the question was how to build a research agenda around that longer-term direction, rather than just follow whichever benchmark was popular at the time.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broader shift toward embodied AI, but it does not say that U.S. reinforcement-learning and computer-vision researchers were converging on it around 2019 when taking faculty positions.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, I saw embodied AI as a promising direction, but not yet a settled one. The question was shifting from “Can a model recognize what is in an image?” to “Can an agent use what it sees to act in the world?” Once you ask that, perception, learning, and control become much harder to separate.

I wouldn’t describe U.S. academia in 2020 as having already made a complete turn toward embodied AI. It was more an emerging research agenda. For me, its appeal was that it exposed problems you could avoid when working only with static datasets: actions change your observations, mistakes have consequences, and success requires more than a good prediction.

So I saw it as a long-term research opportunity. That was the context in which I was thinking about returning to China—not that the direction had already been proven, but that there were still fundamental questions worth building a research program around.

r001.rationale: The response describes embodied AI as an emerging agenda around 2020, but does not say that researchers from reinforcement learning and computer vision were converging on it when taking faculty positions.
